source.title_on_document: Perspective Taking Shapes Creative Performance in Human–AI Collaboration

supplement.where: Appendix, pp. 39-41; Appendix 1: Task Instructions, pp. 42-44. Sections 2.2-2.3 call the latter Online Appendix 1, but it is included in the saved PDF. No separate supplement URL is provided.
supplement.holds: Supplementary Figure 1 (p. 39) shows forward-flow semantic-distance trajectories and role comparisons. Supplementary Table 1 (p. 40) reports PIT immediate-perspective-taking APIM coefficients and standard errors. Supplementary Table 2 (pp. 40-41) reports model fit. Appendix 1 (pp. 42-44) contains participant instructions and AI task, selection and posttest prompts. Main Tables 3 and 5 already contain AUT immediate and PIT delayed APIM coefficients and standard errors (pp. 19, 25).

paper_design_summary: University students were randomly assigned to collaborate with another person or GPT-5-mini in a laboratory and completed rubber-band alternative uses and chair-improvement brainstorming in random task order. Partners took turns contributing ideas while AI remained available in the AI condition; independent raters scored novelty and usefulness, and coders counted ideas and categories. The same experiment reports both dyad performance, which includes AI output in the AI arm, and human-only role comparisons, followed by observational analyses relating perspective taking to performance.

studies.label: Randomized human-AI versus human-human brainstorming: AUT and PIT in the same sample

assignment.what_was_assigned: Human participants were assigned to a human partner (HH) or an AI partner (HAI). The paper describes one between-subjects collaboration-type factor. Both tasks were completed by the same assigned participants in random order; condition assignment did not cross over. The random-sequence generation and allocation-concealment procedures are not stated.
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to the HH or HAI condition, with 57 dyads in the HH condition and 55 dyads in the HAI condition.
assignment.locator: p. 1, Abstract; pp. 8-10, sections 2.1-2.3 (random condition assignment, laboratory setting and random task order)

arms.name: Human-AI collaboration (HAI)
arms.description: One human participant and GPT-5-mini brainstorm through the web chat interface. The human always contributes first. Table 1 gives 55 human participants before task-specific exclusions. Analyzed dyads are HAI (49) for AUT and HAI (54) for PIT; there is no single reported unique-person analysis count across the two tasks, so n_analyzed is left null (pp. 8-10, 15, 17, 21).

arms.name: Human-human collaboration (HH)
arms.description: Two human participants collaborate through the same web interface in separate rooms, after meeting and drawing lots for who speaks first. Table 1 gives 114 human participants before task-specific exclusions. Analyzed dyads are HH (53) for AUT and HH (55) for PIT. These are dyad counts, not people counts; task-specific arm people counts and a unique-person count across tasks are not printed (pp. 8-10, 15, 17, 21).

participants.exclusions: Task-specific analysis samples: 155 people analyzed for AUT and 164 for PIT. The n_analyzed field uses the largest reported task sample (PIT), not a claimed union across tasks. AUT: 14 people excluded; 6 HAI participants (4 instruction violations and 2 network failures), and 4 HH dyads (2 instruction violations and 2 network failures). PIT: 5 people excluded; 1 HAI participant for network failure, and 2 HH dyads (1 instruction violation and 1 network failure). Violations included not producing one idea per turn, copying AI, only questioning AI or off-task chatting; network interruptions produced incomplete records. A participant's valid data in the other task were retained (pp. 8-9, section 2.1). Arm n_analyzed values remain null because counts vary by task and no unique-person total by arm across tasks is given.
participants.who: Students recruited from Central China Normal University; the abstract identifies university students. The two creative tasks use the same recruited sample (p. 1; pp. 8-10).
participants.quote: After excluding participants who did not follow the instructions in each task, 155 participants had valid data for the AUT and 164 for the PIT.
participants.locator: pp. 8-9, section 2.1; p. 1, Abstract and university affiliation in Wuhan, China; p. 15, Table 1; p. 17, Table 2; p. 21, Table 4

ai_tool.how_used: Reciprocal turn-taking brainstorming partner through an API in a custom web chat interface, rather than unrestricted chatbot use: each partner provided one idea per turn, without questions or evaluations, and could send no further idea before the partner responded. Task-specific system prompts matched the human instructions; AI ideas were limited to 40 Chinese characters. AI remained available throughout production of all scored ideas. The human always spoke first in HAI (pp. 9-10, sections 2.2-2.3; pp. 42-43, Appendix 1).

task.description: Two task types within one experiment: Alternative Uses Task (divergent_test), generating unusual uses for a rubber band; and Product Improvement Task (idea_generation), generating creative ways to improve a chair. Participants and partners alternated one idea per turn (pp. 9-10, sections 2.2-2.3; pp. 42-43, Appendix 1).
task.duration: AUT: 10 minutes; PIT: 15 minutes; random task order with a 3-minute break between tasks (p. 10, section 2.3).

outcomes.name: AUT: human participant mean idea novelty
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two graduate students with a creativity-research background independently rated every idea on a 7-point scale using the Consensual Assessment Technique; they were blind to conditions, identities and hypotheses. The two ratings were averaged per idea, then scores were averaged over each participant's own ideas (p. 13, section 2.5). Coded expert_raters because the paper specifies creativity-research training, rather than lay or crowd raters. Role comparisons use linear mixed-effects models; the paper models dyad dependence with random intercepts (p. 14, section 2.6). This record retains the Human in HAI versus Human in HH comparison; AI-generated output is excluded from the human outcome. The APIM analyses concern the same creativity measures with observed perspective-taking predictors and are not additional randomized interventions. AUT analyzed sample: 155 people; Table 2 reports 49 HAI dyads and 53 HH dyads (pp. 8-9, section 2.1; p. 17, Table 2). Figure 3A also plots AI, which is not a human treatment arm. The dyad novelty result in Table 2 is recorded separately.

contrasts.reported: Human in HAI > Human in HH: t(124.63) = 2.58, p = 0.029, d = 0.47. Numerical human-arm means, dispersions and a confidence interval for this contrast are not printed.

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: No external participant reuse is stated. The document describes recruitment for this experiment; AUT and PIT share the experiment's recruited sample and are not independent studies.
sample_overlap.quote: A total of 169 participants were recruited from Central China Normal University.

company_involvement.description: No company authorship, funding or study involvement is stated. Listed affiliations are academic or public research institutions. Use of the GPT-5-mini API and the stated OpenAI-assisted translation is reported, but does not itself establish company involvement.
company_involvement.locator: p. 1, author affiliations and translation note; p. 9, section 2.2

eligibility.reason: People were randomly assigned to AI versus human collaborative assistance (p. 8, section 2.1), and the setting was a laboratory despite the web-based interface (p. 10, section 2.3). Both analyzed samples exceed the threshold: 155 people for AUT and 164 for PIT (pp. 8-9, section 2.1). Novelty and usefulness were independently rated on actual ideas and fluency/flexibility were counted from outputs (p. 13, section 2.5); human-only AI-assisted versus human-partner contrasts are reported (pp. 17, 22, sections 3.2.2 and 3.3.2). The comparator is an active human partner, not unassisted work. AI was available during production, and the role comparisons do not make this an ai_vs_human-only study.

one_line_finding: Humans collaborating with GPT-5-mini generated more novel ideas than humans collaborating with another person in AUT (d = 0.47, p = 0.029; p. 17, section 3.2.2) and PIT (d = 0.42, p = 0.045; p. 22, section 3.3.2).
open_questions: What dispersion do the parenthetical values in Tables 2 and 4 represent? The saved PDF does not explicitly label them SD or SE; do not use them as standard deviations without confirmation.

The unique number of people analyzed on at least one task, and corresponding unique-person arm counts, are not stated. The form reports the largest explicitly stated task sample, 164 for PIT, and retains the smaller AUT sample in the notes.

notes: Screened 2026-10-09. Read the full markdown, including references and all appendices, and checked design, counts and recorded statistics against the corresponding PDF pages. One experiment is coded: its tasks and its human/dyad analyses are dependent, not additional studies. The paper calls novelty, usefulness, fluency and flexibility the primary creative-performance outcomes (p. 9, section 2.2), but does not single out one endpoint or task; paper_primary reflects that designation, not four independent primary estimates. Human-only outcomes are listed first. The form's 15-outcome cap is applied because the paper reports creativity measures at both participant and dyad levels and additional forward-flow analyses. Included are the human-level creativity outcomes for both tasks and the dyad-level creativity outcomes except PIT dyad flexibility. Omitted from the outcome array: PIT dyad flexibility, HAI (54 dyads) 9.84 (2.15) versus HH (55 dyads) 9.10 (1.79), t = 1.96, df = 102.92, d = 0.38, p = 0.053 (p. 21, Table 4 and section 3.3.1); and AUT/PIT forward-flow outcomes shown only in Supplementary Figure 1 (p. 39). Forward flow compares each current idea with all preceding valid ideas in the same dyad and task, rather than comparing independent people's output pools; the caption does not name the semantic model or inferential procedure. No plotted values are estimated. Immediate/delayed perspective taking (pp. 13-14, 17, 21-22) is coded by partner-category overlap and is labeled an interaction-process measure by the paper; it is not an across-people homogenization outcome for independent human outputs. Its APIM predictor effects are associations with the same creativity outcomes, not separately randomized treatments or additional creativity endpoints (pp. 14-15, 19, 25, 40). Questionnaire measures of perspective-taking tendency, creative potential and task experience are self-reports and are excluded. Idea selection is instructed but no separately scored selection outcome is reported. There is no after-AI creative-production phase. The study's AI-role comparisons use AI ideas generated within an actual human-AI interaction, not an independent unassisted AI-output benchmark. Null n_units values avoid deriving combined dyad totals or mistaking model observations including AI for people. Printed d values are preserved without recalculation; the standardizer for these d values is not explicitly identified in the saved PDF. No preregistration, study data URL or code URL is stated.
